summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option, defining two key sizes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2950 specifies how Telnet can encrypt data with CAST-128 in cipher feedback mode. It warns that this mode does not guarantee data integrity and that the 40-bit key variant is not secure.

questions: how does telnet cast-128 cfb64 work
does telnet cfb64 protect data integrity
subtitle: How Telnet uses CAST-128 in 64-bit cipher feedback mode.

tldr.problem: Telnet's encryption option needs a defined way to use CAST-128 in cipher feedback mode with negotiated keys.
tldr.mechanism: The encrypting side sends an 8-byte initial vector, negotiates a key identifier, and then encrypts data using CAST-128 CFB64.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines 40-bit and 128-bit key variants, while warning that cipher feedback does not ensure data integrity and 40-bit keys are not secure.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 2950's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC defines Telnet use of CAST-128 cipher feedback and documents limitations of the mode.

sections.title: Setting Up CAST-128 CFB64
sections.content:
The RFC defines CAST-128 in cipher feedback mode for Telnet's encryption option, with 40-bit and 128-bit key variants. The side that will encrypt generates a random 8-byte initial vector and sends it in clear text to the other side.

After the receiver accepts the vector, the sides negotiate a key identifier. Once they have a common key identifier, the encrypting side can send START and END commands to control encryption. A changed key identifier or initial vector requires the encryption state to be reinitialized.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers exchange an initial vector and agree on a key identifier before encrypting Telnet data. The vector is sent openly, while it helps set the encryption state.

sections.title: How Cipher Feedback Processes Data
sections.content:
The method begins by applying CAST to the initial vector with the key. It combines the resulting state with an input block to produce encrypted output, then feeds that output into the next step.

The RFC also describes how the default key may come from the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option. If there is insufficient key material for a given variant, that encryption option must not be offered or used.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm uses the key and initial vector to transform data in sequence. Both sides need matching key material and state to encrypt and decrypt correctly.

sections.title: Integrity and Key-Size Warnings
sections.content:
The RFC states that cipher feedback encryption does not ensure data integrity. An active attacker may be able to modify text if the clear text is predictable, though the described changes can also corrupt following data.

The document says the 40-bit-key mode is not to be considered secure and is included to document existing implementations. It notes that adding a message authentication code would increase the bytes needed to send a Telnet character.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption alone does not prove that data was left unchanged. The RFC explicitly says the 40-bit version is not secure.
